name: Prussian nationalism
summary: Prussian nationalism is a state nationalism built around the Hohenzollern kingdom: loyalty to the dynasty, a professional army, a service nobility and an orderly bureaucracy, with Protestant identity and duty, discipline and self-denial as its virtues. It favoured concentrating power in Prussia, expanding its territory and leading a small-German state under the crown, and it distrusted parliaments and liberal reform. Toward minorities, notably Poles and Catholics, it pursued assimilation and German-language policy.
scope: Prussia as a state ideology from Frederick William I and Frederick the Great through the Bismarckian unification and the Wilhelmine Reich (c. 1713-1918), covering Prussianism as the conservative, monarchist, militarist tradition of the Junkers and officials. It excludes Nazism's later use of 'Prussian values' and pan-German or liberal German nationalism. Economic, social and modern-issue answers are mostly inferred and low confidence.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Prussian sources discuss schooling and administration, not health care; the paternalist state tradition leans slightly toward provision but nothing in the sources states it.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property was protected for nobles (Frederick bars non-nobles buying noble estates) but the crown also limited it for state ends; no stated absolute-rights stance.

strong-leader.rationale: Frederick holds that policy should come from one mind with the king personally running government; Bismarck likewise set the crown and executive above a gridlocked budget committee.

state-harmful.rationale: The state is the central object of Prussian loyalty; the king is called the first servant of the state, so the claim that the state is harmful is the opposite of the doctrine.

empower-police-military.rationale: Prussianism is defined by militarism, iron discipline and a professional army placed at the centre of state; Bismarck defends the military budget against parliament.

decide-locally.rationale: Prussian reformers built centralising ministries, though the 1808 ordinance gave towns some autonomy; the Junker semifeudal localism was resisted by the crown's centralisation.

traditional-family.rationale: A strictly hierarchical social order built on Pietist religiosity and duty supports traditional family structure, though sources do not cite the family itself.

more-religion-public.rationale: Fear of God heads the list of Prussian social virtues and the court was shaped by Pietism, though Frederick II also confined the clergy within limits.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not a Prussianist concern; a conservative state nationalism that favoured Prussians and Germanised Poles would not embrace active correction.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Prussian nationalism is described as state nationalism that treated Prussians as a nation and promoted their cultural unity, with Protestant identity central.

gradual-change.rationale: Prussian reform came from above via ministries (Stein, Humboldt) and the Junkers kept inherited privileges; Bismarck however openly used force to break the constitutional deadlock.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Prussia itself settled colonists and encouraged German immigration while expelling Poles, so no single position on immigration levels emerges.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Bismarck's speech rests on Prussian power concentration and force, not on supranational bodies; the tradition places the sovereign state at the top.

free-trade.rationale: Frederick's testament uses taxation of trade as leverage and steers merchants for state ends; mercantilist, though later Prussia led a customs union, so low.

nation-first.rationale: Bismarck calls for concentrating Prussia's power and seizing the right moment; Frederick's testament counsels advantage for Prussia amid hostile neighbours.

revolution-justified.rationale: Bismarck defends the crown against parliamentary pressure and Prussian conservatives defended the monarch; Prussianism is counter-revolutionary and loyal to the dynasty.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not a Prussian concept; landed conservatism with private estates points away from worker or public ownership.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Frederick's testament says all financial, political and military matters must flow toward one goal of strengthening the state, supporting state direction of the economy.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Frederick sought to protect peasant holdings from absorption into noble farms but also to keep estates in noble hands; mixed.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Abolishing money and wages is opposite to traditional, hierarchical, conservative Prussianism.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rule was dynastic and personal by the Hohenzollerns, not by a party; party rule is not the model.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

reviewHistory.rationale: Prussian rule was dynastic and personal under the Hohenzollerns and the nationalism grew out of that dynasty's state-building; the monarchy is the defining form.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

democracy-best.rationale: Bismarck says majority votes and speeches do not settle great questions and doubts liberal constitutional government in Prussia; Prussianism opposes parliamentary democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Bismarck dismissed majority votes as an answer to major questions; direct popular votes on laws conflict with the monarchical order.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as the basis of power overturn the vertical, centralised, paternalistic structure of Prussianism.

right-to-secede.rationale: A state nationalism that built and expanded Prussia from Brandenburg and East Prussia treats territorial unity as sacrosanct.

natural-rulers.rationale: Prussianism rests on the conservative military caste of Junkers, whose aristocratic leadership of state and army the crown made indispensable.

political-violence-never.rationale: Bismarck's line that great questions are decided by iron and blood rejects the claim that political violence is never justified.

separate-church-state.rationale: Hohenzollern rulers headed a Protestant state and Bismarck fought the Catholic church in the Kulturkampf, though Frederick II limited the clergy; a strict wall was not the ideal.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Frederick holds that the clergy be confined within due limits and law comes from the sovereign and civil codes like the 1794 code, not scripture.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The professional army and centralised state are the heart of Prussianism; privatising defence is directly opposed.

military-superiority.rationale: Frederick's testament gives detailed instruction on strength and organisation of the army amid hostile neighbours; superiority was the state's survival creed.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Prussia assimilated and Germanised Poles but also admitted Huguenots and Jews, so its nationalism is state-based rather than ethnic and adherents split.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Prussianism upholds hierarchy and service between classes; Marxist class conflict as history's engine contradicts it.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Frederick wants the noble class preserved and the order of ranks kept, so equal outcomes are opposed.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Prussian virtues praise sacrifice, duty and self-denial for the state and king, opposing the claim that self-interest is morally good.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Sense of duty is a core social virtue and the military ethos made self-denial for state and king central; the state is sovereign over the individual.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Prussia built a modern army, bureaucracy and state; the claim is foreign to it.

restore-past-order.rationale: Prussianism is conservative and traditionalist but also modernised through reform and unification, so restoring a lost order is not clearly its core.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Bismarck's realpolitik judged questions by power and outcome rather than doctrine; the framing is modern, so low.

direct-action.rationale: Disciplined hierarchy opposes street direct action, though the question is ambiguous about state actors.

means-match-ends.rationale: Bismarck's iron-and-blood politics and Frederick's amoral treaty policy do not require means to mirror ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Utterly foreign to a state-building, militaristic tradition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Opposed to a hierarchical order of nobles, officers, officials and peasants.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution by need conflicts with a ranked order based on service and rank.

production-for-use.rationale: Not a Prussian idea; the crown directed production for state strength instead.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A revolutionary working-class dictatorship is the opposite of the dynastic, aristocratic Prussian state.

collective-farming.rationale: Frederick wanted to protect individual peasant holdings and noble estates, not collectivise land.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Prussian militarism saw war as statecraft, not a result of capitalism; the thesis is Marxist.

taxation-theft.rationale: The Prussian state lived on taxes and Frederick's testament treats the state's finances as the sovereign's central work; taxation is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: The disciplined, Pietist order held morals and duty above individual liberty alone, so limiting the state to preventing harm is not the doctrine.

conscription.rationale: The army was central to Prussian identity and the Prussian military code extended to the whole Reich in 1871; universal service was its military foundation.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Frederick wanted nobles kept from serving abroad without permission and subjects held to the state; exit is not valued.

state-as-business.rationale: The ruler is first servant of the state, a duty ethic rather than a business model; the framing is modern.

positive-liberty.rationale: A paternalistic state provided schooling and orderly administration, but nothing states a doctrine of material means for freedom.

total-state.rationale: The state was centralised and paternalistic but Frederick tolerated religion and private belief; a totalising state is not the Prussian ideal.

national-rebirth.rationale: Prussianism celebrates an existing dynastic tradition; the radical-rebirth idea belongs to fascism rather than conservative state nationalism.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Frederick's testament names Saxony, Polish Prussia and Swedish Pomerania as desirable acquisitions and Prussia's history was one of expansion across Brandenburg, Silesia and the Rhineland.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule was dynastic and personal, and Junker nobles were tied to the Crown by service in exchange for privileges, though the Reich was constitutional.

bound-labor.rationale: Frederick reduced but kept labour services and serfdom on estates, planning only later to free Silesian serfs; East Elbian Junker estates depended on bound labour.

single-common-good.rationale: Frederick wants all financial, political and military matters to flow toward one goal of state strength under one mind rather than balance competing interests.

revive-national-language.rationale: Prussia suppressed Polish in schools and administration in favour of German; reviving other languages was not its project, though no view on a Prussian language arises.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democratic control of firms conflicts with a vertical paternalistic hierarchy.

school-vouchers.rationale: Prussia built a state school system with most children in formal schooling by the 1840s, so choice via vouchers runs against the state-centred model.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Frederick William I made frugality and order the basis of reforming a heavily indebted state; fiscal discipline is a Prussian virtue.

economic-freedom.rationale: The crown steered the economy for state ends; Prussianism does not tie political order to economic freedom.

national-self-determination.rationale: Prussia asserted its own state and nation yet Prussian Poles and others were denied the right; Bismarck rejected Frankfurt-style popular self-determination.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Fear of God and Pietism stand first among Prussian virtues; Frederick the Great as enlightened ruler is a counterweight.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Prussian policy distinguished subjects and non-citizens, deporting Poles without German citizenship, so reserving benefits is plausible; welfare not directly sourced.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Prussian vertical paternalistic order sees ranks serving the state together; the conservative ideal is cooperation under authority, not class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Prussianism venerates tradition and the inherited institutions of the dynasty; sacrificing heritage is opposed.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Prussia admitted Huguenots, Jews and different Christian confessions under Frederick, and the Prussian state was not racial; racial segregation law is not part of it.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Prussian doctrine presents the state as above classes, a service to the whole, not a ruling class tool, though critics argue otherwise.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Prussian policy replaced Polish with German in administration, courts and schooling and settled German colonists; assimilation was explicit state policy.

proportional-representation.rationale: Bismarck distrusted parliamentary majorities; Prussia's three-class franchise gave unequal weight to property.

national-mission.rationale: Protestant triumphalism is noted but the sources do not show a mission to spread Prussian government; Prussian nationalism looked inward to the state.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The hierarchical social order is not described as an injustice by Prussianism.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Prussian tradition prized an orderly, incorruptible bureaucracy and a service nobility; Incorruptibility is on its list of virtues.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics came later and Clark treats Nazi use of Prussian values as a fetish; not part of the tradition.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Prussian state was an active builder of ministries, schools, courts and army; a minimal state is the opposite.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Prussia pursued cultural assimilation of Poles rather than racial purity; racial endogamy is not its doctrine.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Prussia settled Germans on lands taken from Poles; its adherents would not call that unlawful.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The 1794 Civil Code and a single even-handed judicial system reflect the Prussian ideal of uniform state law, though Frederick tolerated several religions.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Prussia was tolerant of confessions and of Jews, with Protestant missionary hopes; no restriction documented.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Irrelevant to the Prussian tradition; no ban would be sought.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Socialist doctrine; the encirclement logic parallels Frederick's hostile neighbours, but the proposition is not Prussian.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Legitimacy came from the dynasty and Frederick's absolutist view of the sovereign as the state's servant, not consent of the governed.

population-transfer.rationale: The Prussian Settlement Commission bought land for German colonists and 35,000 Poles without German citizenship were deported; pressure on hostile minorities was state policy.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Bismarck says iron and blood decide great questions and Frederick's testament plans acquisitions by opportunism, so initiating force is accepted.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Prussia's expansionist nationalism viewed relations between states as struggle, with Bismarck stressing power; individuals' competition is less central.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The absolutist king's power over subjects was unchecked in Frederick's view; the republican concept is opposed.

separated-powers.rationale: Frederick wants high courts reporting directly to the ruler and policy from one mind; powers are united in the crown.

vanguard-party.rationale: A Leninist party vanguard has no place in the dynastic state tradition.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Public housing estates did not exist in the Prussian kingdom's political debates, and the sources give no basis for a stance on tenant purchase.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Prussian policy sought cultural unity and Germanisation of minorities, treating diversity as a threat to the state, though Frederick tolerated confessions.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Prussia filled posts by service, rank and orderly bureaucracy; lottery contradicts that.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Bismarck argued that without a budget the constitution gave no way out and the crown could act; emergency prerogative is the Prussian line.

party-controls-media.rationale: Rule was dynastic not party-based; press control by the monarchic state is plausible but not a party media model.

party-commands-army.rationale: The army belonged to the king, who ran it almost as a private domain; party command is opposed.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The Prussian state tied political voice to estate and property and rewarded service with rank; the proposal conflicts.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not a Prussian doctrine; party discipline lacked a role in a royal state.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Bismarck wanted Prussian power concentrated; sovereignty was not to be shared with supranational bodies.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The monarch commanded the army as a private domain and the 1871 constitution extended the Prussian military code to the Reich; the head of state commanded the forces.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Prussia's Hohenzollerns were Protestant rulers who headed their church; bishops were not the model and Frederick confined clergy.

clerical-rule.rationale: Frederick holds that the clergy be confined within due limits, and the state is ruled by king and officials, so clerical rule is rejected.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A Marxist defeatist stance is the opposite of Prussian loyalty to king and army.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials answered to the king through the bureaucracy; recall by voters conflicts with that.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Frederick advises an alliance with France and Bismarck's Prussia relied on alliances; ending them runs against the testament's diplomacy.

people-in-arms.rationale: Prussia is the model of the professional army; Prussian reforms did create the citizen army through conscription but kept an officer-corps professional core, so the pure militia is opposed.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Bismarck called for a small German nation-state led by Prussia, so reunification of the Germans was a goal, though under Prussian terms.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Prussia valued education: over 80 percent of children were in school by the 1840s and universities were reformed; hostility to the educated is not its trait.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Prussian officials treated Polish culture as lesser and Prussian order as superior, so cultural equality is not held.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Subjecthood derived from the state and Prussia's policy turned on state not descent, though Poles were excluded from citizenship; adherents split.

minority-language-support.rationale: Prussia replaced Polish with German in administration, courts and schools and dismissed Polish teachers; minority language support was reversed.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Frederick lets many confessions coexist but through state tolerance; no doctrine on exemptions from general law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conformity, order, discipline and self-restraint are Prussian virtues, so social pressure to conform is endorsed.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A post-colonial claim, foreign to Prussianism.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Bismarck rejected parliamentary majorities settling the constitution by speeches and votes; the 1848 Frankfurt route failed in his view.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Frederick's absolutist state directed finances and trade for strength, accepting limits on subjects' liberty for state ends.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state was a hereditary Hohenzollern king; election of the head of state is the opposite.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Bismarck wanted Prussia's borders widened and held lands; giving up claimed territory conflicts with expansion.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Frederick tied noble privilege to service and restricted land transactions to preserve cultivators; property rights were conditional on service to the state.

collective-defense.rationale: Frederick counsels alliances against hostile neighbours; mutual defence follows from that, though Prussia broke treaties when it paid.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Frederick lists neighbouring provinces to acquire by opportunism; annexation without consent was the way Prussia grew.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Frederick holds that the clergy be confined within due limits and Bismarck's Kulturkampf curbed the Catholic Church's power; the state sits above the church.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The Prussian king ruled personally and was involved in running the army and policy; the king was not a ceremonial arbiter.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: A state that built itself by military consolidation would use force to keep its provinces; Bismarck's ideal rested on force.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on general self-government, separate laws or no stated position, not on keeping a distinct economic system, and the statement now asks only whether a region joining a larger state should be free to keep its economic system.

reviewHistory.rationale: Prussia assigned different privileges to provinces (Junkers kept provincial privileges) but pursued uniformity through the Reich; the stance is mixed.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Prussian constitution had a king, an aristocratic upper house and an elected lower house, but Bismarck distrusted parliament's weight; adherents hold some balance.

land-redistribution.rationale: Frederick wanted noble estates kept with nobles and the Junker estates were the base of the caste; breaking them up is opposed.

refugee-return.rationale: Prussia deported Poles; the principle of return is not part of its policy.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Bismarck's small German state excluded Austria so Prussia did not claim all Germans, while territorial claims rested on dynastic interest; mixed.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Frederick's Prussia tolerated many confessions and the state kept clergy in limits; punishing leaving a religion is contrary.

women-must-cover.rationale: No such custom in Prussian Protestantism; opposed.

common-currency.rationale: The Reich later unified currency, but there is no stated view.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Bismarck's small German solution united many Germans under Prussia but excluded Austrians, so adherents split between German union and Prussian state interest.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Prussia suppressed Polish schools and Catholic services under the Kulturkampf and Germanisation; self-governing minority institutions were refused.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Prussianism sees dynasty, state and will as the drivers of history, not modes of production.

ban-cartels.rationale: Cartel law is not mentioned in the sources; the crown directed commerce for state ends but did not address market concentration as such.

no-bailouts.rationale: Frugality supports it but a paternal state aids its own; split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Prussian courts reported to the ruler and were not a check on a majority but no majority rule existed; the question is not Prussian.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Frederick's mercantilist testament seeks economic strength and trade advantage for Prussia, favouring a self-reliant bloc.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding labour and environmental clauses in trade deals are a late twentieth-century device with no Prussian counterpart or documented stance.

moral-incentives.rationale: Honour, duty and self-sacrifice rather than reward are core Prussian virtues, so moral incentives fit; the claim as stated is socialist.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Prussianism is counter-revolutionary; Bismarck defended the crown against revolutionary pressure.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Frederick says the noble class should be preserved and kept apart, and the Junker caste rests on inherited privilege.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Prussian order was contrasted with stereotyped Polish mismanagement and used to justify rule over Poles.

patriotic-education.rationale: Virtues oriented toward service to state and king and Prussia's school system built civic loyalty; the Kulturkampf and Germanisation used schools to teach loyalty to the state.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Bismarck distrusted liberal constitutionalism; the crown held authority above entrenched limits.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Hohenzollern rule is hereditary and dynastic; elective rulers are the opposite.

minority-veto.rationale: Bismarck says great questions are decided by force and state authority; a minority veto cannot bind the sovereign state.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Frederick's state is absolutist and subjects are expected to obey; resistance to the king is not endorsed, although Marwitz's refusal of an order is praised.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Bismarck contended that the Crown acts when parliament gives no budget, and he rejected parliamentary primacy.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Duty to state and king is the central virtue, so withdrawal from public affairs is the opposite.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is foreign to it.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Frederick's testament seeks economic strength by the state's own resources.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Bismarck called Prussia's Vienna borders unfavourable and the state sought to gain territory; recovering lost lands accords.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: A tradition that venerates inherited heritage would keep monuments of its past.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Bismarck argued that Prussia's character did not suit liberal institutions and that other German states could indulge liberalism; each state has its own system.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The army was central to Prussian identity and the 1914 statute put much of Germany under commanding generals; the army guarded order and the constitution.

paid-care-work.rationale: Wages for domestic labour is a modern feminist proposal, and the Prussian sources contain nothing on it either way.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Policy attention to male disadvantage is a contemporary debate that the Prussian sources do not touch.

filial-duty.rationale: A hierarchical society with duty as a core virtue supports lifelong filial duty, though the sources do not cite it directly.

office-by-exam.rationale: Prussia was known for an orderly, increasingly even-handed professional bureaucracy; competence-based entry matches, though noble preference also existed.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Officials answered to the king; binding mandates and recall by constituents contradict that.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Estates held in private noble hands under the crown; communal tenure is opposed.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Bismarck's stance in 1862 was that the Crown could govern without a budget; Prussianism resisted parliament's budget power.

single-official-language.rationale: Prussia replaced Polish with German as the sole language of administration, courts and schooling.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Frugality, modesty and restraint are Prussian virtues and the "be more than appear" motto opposes status display.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: The state treated foreign-influenced minorities as Reichsfeinde and restricted their institutions; restriction is consistent.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Frederick wanted more cultivators and settled colonists to strengthen the state; pronatalism is consistent.

residents-only-property.rationale: The Settlement Commission and bans on Poles building houses were measures to keep land in German hands.

democratic-peace.rationale: Bismarck did not see democracy as a route to peace and Prussia's power politics assumed interests, not regimes, drive war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Obedience is a military virtue and sense of duty a core civic one; no duty to obey is the opposite.

non-intervention.rationale: Frederick plans acquisitions through opportunism and treaty breaking when it benefits; non-intervention is not held.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The state labelled Poles and Catholics Reichsfeinde under Bismarck; this is the closest documented analogue, not an explicit conspiracy theory.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Pietist, hierarchical tradition upholds legal marriage.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Frederick's testament was secret and not printed until 1920 and Bismarck edited it; secrecy in state matters was normal.

informal-organisation.rationale: Opposed to a disciplined hierarchical order.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Frederick advises alliance with France and patient opportunism, not ritual submission, and the sources document no tribute-style system, so this is a weak inference.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Prussia built state schools but also relied on Pietist charity institutions like the Francke Foundation; mixed.

religion-illusion.rationale: Pietism shaped the Prussian court and fear of God heads the Prussian virtue list (s6), so the tradition rejects religion as an illusion, though Frederick II himself was a Voltairean sceptic.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: A Marxist claim opposed to conservative Prussianism.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Prussia promoted German over Polish but did not campaign against loanwords in the sources; no position.

treaties-binding.rationale: Frederick advises breaking treaties only rarely and when advantage permits, so treaties are not absolutely binding on Prussia.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Contrary to a centralised hierarchical state.

majority-settlement.rationale: The Prussian Settlement Commission bought Polish land for German colonists in Posen, a state policy of settling the majority group in minority regions.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The state tradition did not deny it; Clark treats Nazi use of Prussian values as a fetish, not an extension.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Bismarck defended governing against the parliamentary majority and the Kulturkampf suppressed Catholic organisations.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The king was the head of the state and church; clerical removal of rulers is opposed.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Bismarck distrusted popular input and dismissed majority votes; participation is not the model.

alienated-labor.rationale: Diligence and duty exalt labour; the Marxist critique is foreign.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Islam in Western countries is a modern debate; Frederick's testament lists tolerated Christian and Jewish confessions but gives no stance on Muslims.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Employment nondisclosure agreements and arbitration are modern legal devices, with no Prussian sources addressing them.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Militarism and a professional army are the essence of Prussianism; abolition is its opposite.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Frederick advises alliances such as with France against Austria; neutrality is not the doctrine, though he also counsels patient waiting.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Rule was dynastic and hereditary under the Hohenzollerns; succession by one's child is the basic principle.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Frugality and fiscal discipline are virtues; refusing austerity conflicts with them.

property-franchise.rationale: The Prussian three-class franchise weighted votes by tax paid and the 1808 ordinance tied citizenship to property; this was the Prussian settlement though sources only cite the ordinance.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The 1794 Civil Code and an even-handed judicial system reflect the Rechtsstaat ideal of publicly known laws, though the king remained above.

online-participation.rationale: Internet deliberation is a modern idea and Prussian sources give no basis for a stance.

open-government-data.rationale: Frederick's testament stayed unpublished until 1920 and secrecy was a principle of state; transparency opposed.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Frederick tolerated many faiths, but the Protestant state did privilege Protestant identity; no stated position.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Randomly chosen citizens deliberating contradicts hierarchical service-based rule.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Junker landed elite was protected by the crown, so no worry about wealth concentration emerges.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Fear of God heads the list of Prussian virtues; state atheism is the opposite.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Iron discipline, centralised authority and a militarised state oppose abolition.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Prussia ruled Poles and Catholics through assimilation and Kulturkampf, not shared executive power.

term-limits.rationale: Hereditary monarchy and a bureaucracy of long service give no place to term limits.

vote-delegation.rationale: Contrary to hierarchical rule through officials.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk as a policy priority is a recent concern, and the Prussian sources do not reach it.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Protestant traditional order in the period did not include it.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Prussia excluded Poles without citizenship; local vote for foreigners is opposed.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Military virtues and drill shape the tradition and Prussian cadet schools gathered young nobles; uniformed youth is consistent.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The landed estates of the Junkers rewarded ownership; the claim is Marxist-adjacent.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Prussian nationalism traces state-building continuity from the Hohenzollern merger of Brandenburg and East Prussia in the 16th century to the German empire.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Pietist religion is present but the politics was one of power and state interest; split.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: A homeland serving a diaspora is not a Prussian theme; the sources discuss territorial state, not a scattered nation.

culture-before-state.rationale: Prussian nationalism arose from state-building by the Hohenzollern dynasty; the state came first and the national culture was promoted from above.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Settlement Commission land buying and German officials and tradespeople in Polish provinces aimed at German economic dominance.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The state ran many services but no position on local essentials is documented; 1808 Town Ordinance gave towns autonomy.

second-chamber.rationale: The Prussian and imperial systems had an upper house of aristocratic members to check the lower house, and mixed constitution ideas are conservative.

municipal-property.rationale: The 1808 Town Ordinance strengthened municipal autonomy but with property-based citizenship; collective municipal ownership of production is not Prussian.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Bismarck favoured Prussian leadership in a federal state; confederation of towns is opposed.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Research into ageing is a modern topic that the sources do not touch.

person-over-state.rationale: Spengler's "the whole is sovereign" and the state as the reference point of virtue place the state above the person. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Pietist fear of God and the Prussian virtues presume a spiritual side; politics serving it is less stated.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Provincial privileges of the Junkers existed at the crown's pleasure and the centralised state could override them.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Prussian nationalism is state-based and assimilated Poles rather than organising racial groups; Clark treats racial Prussianism as a later Nazi fetish.

racial-pride.rationale: Pride in the Prussian state and nation is present; race pride is not a Prussian concept.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Frederick's testament plans acquisitions of Saxony, Polish Prussia and Swedish Pomerania; wars were not only defensive.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Prussian nationalism treated Prussians as a nation defined by state and dynasty, and Konstantin Franz accused Bismarck of departing from German language-based nationalism.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on whether a foreign plot is believed to exist, or on foreign hostility in general rather than territorial partition, and the statement now asks whether preventing foreign-backed partition should be a central aim of national policy.

reviewHistory.rationale: Frederick's testament sees Prussia surrounded by hostile neighbours, Austria the chief enemy, so the fear of encirclement is native to it.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on whether a foreign plot is believed to exist, or on foreign hostility in general rather than territorial partition, and the statement now asks whether preventing foreign-backed partition should be a central aim of national policy.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

free-public-college.rationale: Prussia built state schools and universities but no stated view on tuition.

arms-reduction.rationale: Frederick wants military discipline and strength kept up and Bismarck defends the military budget; reducing arms is opposed.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Frederick's testament counsels secrecy and opportunism in foreign policy and was withheld from print until 1920.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The state and army as the bearers of arms and Prussian discipline fit a state monopoly of force.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Obedience, loyalty and subordination are military virtues; refusing orders is opposed, although Marwitz's refusal is praised.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Frugality and the experience of reforming a heavily indebted state support limits on borrowing.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Prussianism is the exaltation of the state machine of army and bureaucracy; smashing it is the opposite.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The crown directed the economy toward one goal; free experiment contradicts it.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Natural capital accounting is a recent economic idea absent from the Prussian sources.

sacred-nation.rationale: The state is sovereign and virtue demands sacrifice for it, with the whole above its members; sacredness is not explicit.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The Prussian government treated its Polish provinces as parts of the state; the claim is hostile to centre-led states.

public-service-media.rationale: Publicly funded independent broadcasters did not exist, and the Prussian sources do not describe a stance on press independence beyond state control.

workers-own-party.rationale: Opposed to class parties; Prussian order sought cooperation under the crown.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Liability of polluters for physical harm is a modern legal question the sources never touch.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Environmental priority over liberty is a modern conflict, and the sources give no basis for placing Prussianism on it.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Bravery, loyalty and martial duty are core Prussian virtues, so a pacifist refusal to kill even in defence is rejected.

national-church-status.rationale: Prussian nationalism had a Protestant identity and the crown headed the state church, though Frederick tolerated other faiths.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Toward Poles and other minorities Prussia pursued Germanisation and assimilation, not territorial autonomy.

simple-living.rationale: Frugality, self-denial and modest needs are listed among the Prussian virtues.

self-ownership.rationale: Prussianism stressed obedience, discipline and service to the state, with a paternalistic vertical order rather than individual rights.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Bismarck and the Prussian crown distrusted parliaments and parties and relied on the crown and bureaucracy.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Protestant identity was central, and the state fought Catholics in the Kulturkampf, so denominational lines shaped politics.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Prussianism stressed obedience, duty and royal authority, and Bismarck held that power and state decision, not individual conscience, settle questions.

missingStatements.text: The army should answer to the head of state rather than to parliament.
missingStatements.rationale: The Prussian king ran the army as a near-private domain and Bismarck defended the military budget against the parliament.

missingStatements.text: Nobles and landowners should serve the state as officers and officials in return for keeping their privileges.
missingStatements.rationale: Junkers were drawn into state and military service in exchange for their provincial privileges, and Frederick wanted nobles in army service.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to Prussian state service; not a position other ideologies widely take a side on.

notes: Prussian nationalism overlaps heavily with German conservatism and Bismarckian small-German nationalism; the source Wikipedia article is a stub, so Prussianism, primary texts and a scholarly review carry most of the evidence. Answers on economics, welfare and modern social issues are inferences.
